<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

</ol></li>

<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="p1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="463.6" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 670 463.6" width="670"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,463.6) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#FFFFFF;" fill="#FFFFFF" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 13.84 L 0 449.76 C 0 457.4 6.19 463.6 13.84 463.6 L 656.16 463.6 C 663.81 463.6 670 457.4 670 449.76 L 670 13.84 C 670 6.19 663.81 0 656.16 0 L 13.84 0 C 6.19 0 0 6.19 0 13.84 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#FAF5F5;" fill="#FAF5F5" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 13.84 L 0 449.76 C 0 457.4 6.19 463.6 13.84 463.6 L 656.16 463.6 C 663.81 463.6 670 457.4 670 449.76 L 670 13.84 C 670 6.19 663.81 0 656.16 0 L 13.84 0 C 6.19 0 0 6.19 0 13.84 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 27.67 27.67)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:44.42em;--ltx-fo-height:29.5em;--ltx-fo-depth:0em;font-size:10pt;" height="408.25" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 408.25)" width="614.65"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content"><span id="p1.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-logical-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:44.42em;">
<span id="p1.pic1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<span id="p1.pic1.p2.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="p1.pic1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Decoding as Optimisation on the Probability Simplex:</span></span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p2.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="p1.pic1.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#666666;">From Top-K to Top-P (Nucleus) to Best-of-K Samplers</span></span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p2.3" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="p1.pic1.p2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Xiaotong Ji<sup id="p1.pic1.p2.3.1.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="p1.pic1.p2.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">1,†</span></sup>, Rasul Tutunov<sup id="p1.pic1.p2.3.1.2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="p1.pic1.p2.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">1</span></sup>, Matthieu Zimmer<sup id="p1.pic1.p2.3.1.3" class="ltx_sup"><span id="p1.pic1.p2.3.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">1</span></sup>, Haitham Bou-Ammar<sup id="p1.pic1.p2.3.1.4" class="ltx_sup"><span id="p1.pic1.p2.3.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">1,2,†</span></sup>
<br class="ltx_break"><sup id="p1.pic1.p2.3.1.5" class="ltx_sup"><span id="p1.pic1.p2.3.1.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">1</span></sup></span><span id="p1.pic1.p2.3.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> Huawei Noah’s Ark</span><span id="p1.pic1.p2.3.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><math id="p1.pic1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ {}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow></mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000" mathsize="0.900em">2</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ {}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="p1.pic1.p2.3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> AI Centre, Department of Computer Science, UCL
<br class="ltx_break"><math id="p1.pic1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\dagger" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">†</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\dagger</annotation></semantics></math> Equal contributions</span></span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p2.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.pic1.p2.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Abstract:<span id="p1.pic1.p2.4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
Decoding sits between a language model and everything we do with it, yet it is still treated as a heuristic knob-tuning exercise. We argue decoding should be understood as a principled optimisation layer: at each token, we solve a regularised problem over the probability simplex that trades off model score against structural preferences and constraints. This single template recovers greedy decoding, Softmax sampling, Top-K, Top-P, and Sparsemax-style sparsity as special cases, and explains their common structure through optimality conditions.</span></span></span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p2.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.pic1.p2.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">More importantly, the framework makes it easy to invent new decoders without folklore. We demonstrate this by designing Best-of-K (BoK), a KL-anchored coverage objective aimed at multi-sample pipelines (self-consistency, reranking, verifier selection). BoK targets the probability of covering good alternatives within a fixed K-sample budget and improves empirical performance. We show that such samples can improve accuracy by, for example, +18.6% for Qwen2.5-Math-7B on MATH500 at high sampling temperatures.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="p1.pic1.p1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" color="#000000" height="61.26" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 614.65 61.26" width="614.65"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,61.26) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 7.87 L 0 53.38 C 0 57.73 3.53 61.26 7.87 61.26 L 606.78 61.26 C 611.13 61.26 614.65 57.73 614.65 53.38 L 614.65 7.87 C 614.65 3.53 611.13 0 606.78 0 L 7.87 0 C 3.53 0 0 3.53 0 7.87 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#FCFCFC;" fill="#FCFCFC" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 7.87 L 0 53.38 C 0 57.73 3.53 61.26 7.87 61.26 L 606.78 61.26 C 611.13 61.26 614.65 57.73 614.65 53.38 L 614.65 7.87 C 614.65 3.53 611.13 0 606.78 0 L 7.87 0 C 3.53 0 0 3.53 0 7.87 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#D9D9D9;--ltx-fill-color:#D9D9D9;--ltx-fg-color:#D9D9D9;" color="#D9D9D9" fill="#D9D9D9" stroke="#D9D9D9" stroke-width="2.0pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 1.38 61.26 L 1.38 0"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 15.75 43.77)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:42.15em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:2.59em;font-size:10pt;" height="45.51" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="583.24"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="p1.pic1.p1.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:42.15em;">
<span id="p1.pic1.p1.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="p1.pic1.p1.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="position:relative; bottom:0.2pt;--ltx-fg-color:#1A1A1A;"><img src="" id="p1.pic1.p1.pic1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_missing ltx_missing_image" alt="[Uncaptioned image]"></span><span id="p1.pic1.p1.pic1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#1A1A1A;"> 
Our message is simple: Decoding is not a hack; it is optimisation!
</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_section" style="font-size:144%;">1  Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language model (LLM) decoding is usually taught like a cookbook: Top-K <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>, <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>, temperature <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite>, Top-P <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>, greedy <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>, <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">32</a>]</cite>, beam search <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>]</cite>; a shelf of “tricks” you pick from depending on the application<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>, <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>, <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>, <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>, <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>, <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>, whether you want more determinism <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>, more diversity <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>, <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>, <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>, or fewer hallucinations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>, <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>. The problem is that this framing makes decoding feel like a bag of heuristics: useful, but conceptually disconnected from the rest of machine learning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This paper argues the opposite: many decoding strategies are not heuristics at all. They are solutions to explicit optimisation problems, often the same optimisation problem, with different regularisers and constraints. Once you see decoding through that lens, familiar algorithms stop looking like folklore and start looking like principled design choices. Greedy decoding becomes a limiting case of an objective with no regularisation. Softmax sampling becomes the unique optimum of a score-maximisation problem regularised by (negative) Shannon entropy. Sparsity-inducing decoders arise from alternative convex penalties. In short: decoders differ less by “how they sample” and more by “what objective they are implicitly optimising.”</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our starting point is a small, but surprisingly powerful, shift in perspective. A decoder does not have to immediately choose a token. At each step, it can first choose a distribution over tokens, and only then sample (or take the mode). This turns decoding into a clean optimisation problem over the probability simplex: pick a distribution that (i) puts mass on high-scoring tokens while (ii) satisfying desirable structural preferences such as smoothness, sparsity, or staying close to a reference distribution. This “distribution-first” view is general enough to cover deterministic and stochastic decoding in one line, and it exposes what decoding algorithms do: they are trading off score against regularisation under simplex constraints.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">With that formulation in place, we do something that decoder discussions rarely do: we derive the optimality conditions carefully. Because the variable is a probability distribution, constraints are not decorative; they shape the solution. The simplex geometry introduces the familiar “active vs inactive” behaviour: tokens assigned a nonzero probability satisfy an equality condition, while tokens pushed to zero satisfy an inequality. These KKT-style conditions act like a master key: once derived, you can plug in a choice of regulariser and immediately recover the structure of the decoder it implies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We then use this master key to re-derive canonical decoding rules as special cases. Setting the regulariser weight to zero collapses the optimisation to a linear objective on the simplex, recovering greedy decoding. Choosing negative entropy yields a smooth interior optimum and produces the softmax distribution as a closed-form solution, where temperature sampling is not a hack; it is the optimiser of a maximum-entropy-regularised objective. More broadly, this paper builds the intuition that “decoding methods” are best understood as regularisation families, rather than as unrelated procedures. The takeaway is simple: decoding is an optimisation layer sitting on top of the model’s scores. More precisely, decoding is a convex optimisation problem whose geometry is determined by the choice of regulariser. Once we treat it that way, we gain a principled vocabulary for designing new decoders: decide the behaviour (diversity, sparsity, conservatism, stability), encode it as a regulariser or constraint, and let the resulting optimisation problem define the algorithm.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond theoretical unification, our framework serves as a generative tool for designing next-generation decoding objectives. We exemplify this by addressing the inefficiencies in current multi-sample pipelines through the design of Best-of-K (BoK). Unlike traditional methods that rely on empirical folklore, BoK utilises a KL-anchored coverage objective to maximise the likelihood of capturing high-quality candidates within a constrained K-sample budget. Our results demonstrate that by optimising for coverage, BoK not only provides a more principled decoding path but also achieves improved practical performance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">Across two 7B Qwen models (a math-specialised variant and a general-purpose variant) and three complementary benchmarks, MATH500, GPQA-diamond, and HumanEval, BoK samplers act as a practical decoding-time regulariser that improves multi-sample generation without any extra training or external verifiers. Sweeping temperature from near-deterministic (<math id="S1.p7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau{=}0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau{=}0.1</annotation></semantics></math>) to highly stochastic (<math id="S1.p7.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau{=}0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau{=}0.9</annotation></semantics></math>), BoK samplers consistently match or outperform standard sampling and Top-K, with the largest gains precisely where vanilla sampling is most diverse but least reliable. For example, on the math-specialised model at <math id="S1.p7.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau{=}0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau{=}0.9</annotation></semantics></math> on MATH500, BoK raises accuracy from 53.0% (Base) to 71.6% (+18.6%), exceeding Top-K (56.2%) by +15.4%; similar high-temperature gains appear on GPQA (+6.06%) and HumanEval (+14.64%). These improvements are robust across a range of <math id="S1.p7.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\beta,\lambda)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>λ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\beta,\lambda)</annotation></semantics></math> choices (coverage vs. KL anchoring), indicating a stable operating region rather than brittle tuning. Finally, BoK’s benefits come with only modest compute overhead: using 5 mirror-ascent steps per token adds about 1s on MATH500 (16.88s vs. 15.84s), while even 2 steps already yield a sizeable jump (64.4%→69.6%) with negligible runtime increase—suggesting fast solver convergence and making BoK viable as a lightweight drop-in for practical decoding.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p8.1" class="ltx_p">In short, our contributions can be stated as:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p9" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S1.p9.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="257.84" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 670 257.84" <span id="S1.p9.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:44.66em;">
<span id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<span id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<span id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Unified Theory of Decoding:</span><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> We unify decoding strategies into a single framework, proving they are closed-form optima of objectives on the simplex.</span></span>
</span></span>
<span id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<span id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Generative ”Master Key” for Decoder Design:</span><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> A general framework for automatically deriving iterative algorithms for any decoding behaviour expressed as a regulariser, enabling optimisation beyond closed-form solutions.</span></span>
</span></span>
<span id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<span id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Case Study - Best-of-K (BoK) Decoding:</span><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> We introduce Best-of-K (BoK), a coverage-based objective for self-consistency and reranking. It replaces heuristic sampling with a mathematically grounded approach that improves performance.</span></span>
</span></span>
</span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_section" style="font-size:144%;">2  Decoding, Sampling and Optimisation</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our central claim is that decoding strategies are not heuristics, but rather implicit solutions to well-defined optimisation problems. Sampling-based methods do not introduce randomness arbitrarily; instead, they correspond to soft or regularised forms of optimisation. Conversely, deterministic methods such as greedy arise as limiting or approximate solutions to hard optimisation objectives. From this perspective, decoding algorithms differ <em id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">not in kind</em>, but in what they optimise and the constraints they impose.</p>
</div>

-91.72 297.83 -91.72 Z M 251.97 -97.26"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#D9D9D9;" stroke="#D9D9D9" stroke-width="1.0pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M -275.59 -55.12 L -275.59 -86.61"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#CCCCCC;" fill="#CCCCCC"><path style="stroke:none" d="M -272.82 -55.12 C -272.82 -53.59 -274.06 -52.35 -275.59 -52.35 C -277.12 -52.35 -278.36 -53.59 -278.36 -55.12 C -278.36 -56.65 -277.12 -57.89 -275.59 -57.89 C -274.06 -57.89 -272.82 -56.65 -272.82 -55.12 Z M -275.59 -55.12"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#D9D9D9;" stroke="#D9D9D9"
