-53.59 -136.27 -52.35 -137.8 -52.35 C -139.32 -52.35 -140.56 -53.59 -140.56 -55.12 C -140.56 -56.65 -139.32 -57.89 -137.8 -57.89 C -136.27 -57.89 -135.03 -56.65 -135.03 -55.12 Z M -137.8 -55.12"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#D9D9D9;" stroke="#D9D9D9" stroke-width="1.0pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 0 -55.12 L 0 -86.61"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#CCCCCC;" fill="#CCCCCC"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 2.77 -55.12 C 2.77 -53.59 1.53 -52.35 0 -52.35 C -1.53 -52.35 -2.77 -53.59 -2.77 -55.12 C -2.77 -56.65 -1.53 -57.89 0 -57.89 C 1.53 -57.89 2.77 -56.65 2.77 -55.12 Z M 0 -55.12"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#D9D9D9;" stroke="#D9D9D9" stroke-width="1.0pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 137.8 -55.12 L 137.8 -86.61"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#CCCCCC;" fill="#CCCCCC"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 140.56 -55.12 C 140.56 -53.59 139.32 -52.35 137.8 -52.35 C 136.27 -52.35 135.03 -53.59 135.03 -55.12 C 135.03 -56.65 136.27 -57.89 137.8 -57.89 C 139.32 -57.89 140.56 -56.65 140.56 -55.12 Z M 137.8 -55.12"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#D9D9D9;" stroke="#D9D9D9" stroke-width="1.0pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 275.59 -55.12 L 275.59 -86.61"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#CCCCCC;" fill="#CCCCCC"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 278.36 -55.12 C 278.36 -53.59 277.12 -52.35 275.59 -52.35 C 274.06 -52.35 272.82 -53.59 272.82 -55.12 C 272.82 -56.65 274.06 -57.89 275.59 -57.89 C 277.12 -57.89 278.36 -56.65 278.36 -55.12 Z M 275.59 -55.12"></path></g></g></g></g></svg></span></span></p>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S2.F1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Framework of Decoding as Optimisation: The master objective generalises standard LLM decoding strategies. By choosing appropriate <math id="S2.F1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda,\Omega(q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda,\Omega(q)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, we can recover current decoding strategies as special cases.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The goal of this section is to make this connection explicit. We begin by formalising decoding as the problem of selecting a distribution over next tokens, rather than directly selecting a token. This shift allows us to express decoding as an optimisation problem over distributions, balancing model score and regularisation. We then show that common decoding strategies emerge naturally as special cases.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection" style="font-size:120%;--ltx-fg-color:#808080;">2.1  Decoding as a Decision Over Distributions</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To make the optimisation perspective precise, we start by formalising what a decoder actually does at a single generation step. Consider a language model with parameters <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>𝜽</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math>. Given a prefix <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{x}_{&lt;t}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{t-1})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝒙</mi><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{x}_{&lt;t}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{t-1})</annotation></semantics></math>, the model produces a real-valued score for every token <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> in the vocabulary <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math>. In practice, these scores are the logits or log-probabilities produced by the model. We denote them by: <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}(v)\in\mathbb{R}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi>ℝ</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}(v)\in\mathbb{R}</annotation></semantics></math>, for <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v\in\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v\in\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At this point, most decoding descriptions implicitly assume that we must immediately choose a single token <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. Instead, in this work, we take a small but crucial conceptual step back. Rather than asking which token to select, we ask:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.Ex1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><span id="S2.Ex1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">Which <em id="S2.Ex1.2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_underline ltx_font_italic">distribution over tokens</em> should we use to make the selection?</span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Formally, we introduce an auxiliary distribution <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}(\cdot)\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}(\cdot)\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta(\mathcal{V})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta(\mathcal{V})</annotation></semantics></math> denoting the probability simplex over the vocabulary <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math>. Once <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> is chosen, decoding proceeds by either:</p>
<ul id="S2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">sampling <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}\sim q_{t}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}\sim q_{t}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math>, or</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">deterministically selecting <math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}\in\arg\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}}q_{t}(v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msub><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}\in\arg\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}}q_{t}(v)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.3" class="ltx_p">Importantly, this viewpoint is general enough to cover both stochastic and deterministic decoding, whereby <span id="S2.SS1.p2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i)</span> greedy decoding corresponds to a degenerate distribution <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> that places all its mass on a single token <span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            Please note we assume a rule that breaks ties.</span></span></span>, while <span id="S2.SS1.p2.3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ii)</span> sampling-based decoding corresponds to a non-degenerate <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> with positive entropy. To illustrate this distinction, consider a simple example with a vocabulary of three tokens: <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{V}=\{a,b,c\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{V}=\{a,b,c\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Suppose that, for a given prefix <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, the language model scores each token as follows:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle s_{t}(a)=3,\quad s_{t}(b)=2,\quad s_{t}(c)=0." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle s_{t}(a)=3,\quad s_{t}(b)=2,\quad s_{t}(c)=0.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.4" class="ltx_p">Now, greedy decoding selects the highest-scoring token:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a\in\arg\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}}s_{t}(v)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><munder><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow></munder></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a\in\arg\max_{v\in\mathcal{V}}s_{t}(v).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In our framework, this corresponds to choosing a degenerate distribution <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> that places all its probability mass on the maximiser of the score function:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx3" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.Ex4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle q_{t}(v)=\begin{cases}1,&amp;\text{if }v\in\arg\max\limits_{u}\,s_{t}(u),\\
0,&amp;\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><munder><mi>max</mi><mi>u</mi></munder></mrow><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mtext>otherwise.</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle q_{t}(v)=\begin{cases}1,&amp;\text{if }v\in\arg\max\limits_{u}\,s_{t}(u),\\
0,&amp;\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">In the example above, since <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}(a)&gt;s_{t}(b)&gt;s_{t}(c)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}(a)&gt;s_{t}(b)&gt;s_{t}(c)</annotation></semantics></math>, this reduces to:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx4" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.Ex5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle q_{t}(a)=1,\quad q_{t}(b)=0,\quad q_{t}(c)=0." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle q_{t}(a)=1,\quad q_{t}(b)=0,\quad q_{t}(c)=0.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.3" class="ltx_p">By contrast, sampling-based decoding selects a non-degenerate distribution that assigns nonzero probability to multiple tokens, while still favouring higher-scoring ones. In our framework, such a distribution is also obtained as a function of the score vector <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. Concretely, for a given temperature parameter <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau&gt;0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau&gt;0</annotation></semantics></math>, sampling-based decoding chooses:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}(v)=\frac{\exp(s_{t}(v)/\tau)}{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(s_{t}(u)/\tau)}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>/</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}(v)=\frac{\exp(s_{t}(v)/\tau)}{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{V}}\exp(s_{t}(u)/\tau)},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.4" class="ltx_p">which assigns higher probability to tokens with larger scores, while maintaining positive entropy. In the example above, with scores <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}(a)=3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}(a)=3</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}(b)=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}(b)=2</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}(c)=0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}(c)=0</annotation></semantics></math>, this construction yields a distribution of the form:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx5" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.Ex7"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle q_{t}(a)\approx 0.6,\quad\ q_{t}(b)\approx 0.3,\quad\ \ \ q_{t}(c)\approx 0," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.6</mn></mrow><mo rspace="1.667em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow><mo rspace="2.667em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≈</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle q_{t}(a)\approx 0.6,\quad\ q_{t}(b)\approx 0.3,\quad\ \ \ q_{t}(c)\approx 0,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.5" class="ltx_p">for an appropriate choice of <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>. As such, sampling from <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> will most often select the highest-scoring token <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>a</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a</annotation></semantics></math>, but will occasionally produce <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="b" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>b</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">b</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S2.SS1.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>. This stochasticity allows the decoder to explore alternative continuations while remaining aligned with the model’s scoring function.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Up to this point, common decoding strategies such as greedy decoding and temperature-based sampling may still appear as largely heuristic choices: practical rules that users select and tune based on empirical behaviour or trial-and-error. From this perspective, the decoder is seen as a sampler whose properties, e.g., determinism, diversity, or randomness, are controlled by externally chosen parameters such as temperature. In the next section, we show that this view is <em id="S2.SS1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">incomplete if not misleading</em>. In fact, these decoding strategies are not heuristic procedures, but rather exact solutions to well-defined optimisation problems. Greedy decoding and temperature-based sampling emerge naturally as optimisers of a common objective that trades off expected model score against regularisation. The apparent differences between decoding methods are therefore not algorithmic accidents, but reflect differences in the underlying objectives being optimised.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">This perspective enables a shift in how decoding strategies are designed and understood. Rather than treating samplers as ad-hoc mechanisms, we can view them as solutions to optimisation problems over distributions. Under this lens, designing a decoder with desired properties such as increased diversity, robustness, or constraint satisfaction reduces to specifying the appropriate optimisation objective and constraints. We now make this connection explicit.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection" style="font-size:120%;--ltx-fg-color:#808080;">2.2  Decoding as Distributional Optimisation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The discussion so far suggests that decoding can be viewed as a decision over distributions rather than individual tokens. We now make this perspective explicit by introducing a general optimisation formulation that subsumes a wide range of decoding strategies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">At a given decoding step <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, recall that the model assigns a score <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}(v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}(v)</annotation></semantics></math> to each token <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v\in\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v\in\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math>. We seek to choose a distribution <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}(\cdot)\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}(\cdot)\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})</annotation></semantics></math> from which the next token will be drawn (or whose mode will be selected). We define decoding as the solution to the following optimisation problem:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{\scriptsize\color[rgb]{0.0508,0.2773,0.6328}``Master Problem''}\quad\boxed{q_{t}^{\ast}\;=\;\arg\max_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\Big[\langle q,s_{t}\rangle\;-\;\lambda\,\Omega(q)\Big]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad q\in\mathcal{C}_{t}.}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext style="--ltx-fg-color:#0D47A1;" class="ltx_font_smallcaps" mathcolor="#0D47A1" mathsize="0.700em">“Master Problem”</mtext><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><menclose notation="box"><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>∗</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0.558em" rspace="0.558em">=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.502em">−</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mtext>s.t.</mtext><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow></menclose></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{\scriptsize\color[rgb]{0.0508,0.2773,0.6328}``Master Problem''}\quad\boxed{q_{t}^{\ast}\;=\;\arg\max_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\Big[\langle q,s_{t}\rangle\;-\;\lambda\,\Omega(q)\Big]\quad\text{s.t.}\quad q\in\mathcal{C}_{t}.}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In the above equation, <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\langle q,s_{t}\rangle\;=\;\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}q(v)\,s_{t}(v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.280em" stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.391em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\langle q,s_{t}\rangle\;=\;\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}q(v)\,s_{t}(v)</annotation></semantics></math>, as the expected model’s score under the distribution <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega(q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega(q)</annotation></semantics></math> is a regularisation functional that encodes preferences such as diversity, sparsity, or stability. Moreover, <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> controls the strength of regularisation, and <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes constraints on the support of <math id="S2.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">From a geometric perspective, each component of the formulation plays a structural role. The simplex constraints induce boundary behaviour: tokens may become active or inactive depending on whether the optimiser settles in the interior or on a face of the feasible set. Different choices of regulariser shape this geometry in different ways: some encourage interior solutions, while others allow the optimiser to concentrate mass on lower-dimensional faces. Likewise, hard support constraints restrict the feasible region itself, carving out sub-simplices before optimisation even begins. As we will see in Section <a href="#S3" title="3 LLM Decoding Strategies are Different Regularisers" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, classical decoding rules correspond to particular geometric choices within this framework.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Interpreting Equation (<a href="#S2.E1" title="In 2.2 Decoding as Distributional Optimisation ‣ 2 Decoding, Sampling and Optimisation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The objective above consists of two competing terms. The first term, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\langle q,s_{t}\rangle" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\langle q,s_{t}\rangle</annotation></semantics></math>, encourages the decoder to place probability mass on tokens with high model scores. If this term were optimised alone, the resulting distribution would collapse onto the highest-scoring token. The second term, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega(q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega(q)</annotation></semantics></math>, acts as a regulariser that penalises certain properties of the distribution <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math>. Its role is to control the shape of the decoding distribution, for example, by encouraging diversity or limiting deviation from a reference distribution. The scalar <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> determines the trade-off between strictly optimising model score and satisfying these additional preferences. Finally, the constraint set <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> allows the decoder to enforce hard restrictions, such as limiting the support to a subset of tokens or excluding invalid continuations. Under this view, the design of a decoding strategy reduces to:</p>
<ol id="S2.I2" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S2.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">What notion of quality is being optimised (through <math id="S2.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}(v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}(v)</annotation></semantics></math>);</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">What properties are desired in the decoding distribution (through <math id="S2.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega(q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega(q)</annotation></semantics></math>); and</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">What hard constraints must be respected (through <math id="S2.I2.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Deriving Solution Conditions for Equation (<a href="#S2.E1" title="In 2.2 Decoding as Distributional Optimisation ‣ 2 Decoding, Sampling and Optimisation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Deriving the closed-form solution conditions for our general optimisation problem is relatively involved. We present it in steps that make various assumptions about <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta(q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta(q)</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega(q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega(q)</annotation></semantics></math>. In the first case, we consider the absence of <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. Here, our optimisation problem becomes the following:</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}^{\star}=\arg\max_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\left(\langle q,s_{t}\rangle-\lambda\Omega(q)\right),\ \ \text{for $\lambda\geq 0$}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mtext>for </mtext><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}^{\star}=\arg\max_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\left(\langle q,s_{t}\rangle-\lambda\Omega(q)\right),\ \ \text{for $\lambda\geq 0$},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta(\mathcal{V})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta(\mathcal{V})</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as: <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\Delta(\mathcal{V})=\left\{q\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}:q(v)\geq 0,\sum_{v}q(v)=1\right\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></msup><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>v</mi></msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta(\mathcal{V})=\left\{q\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}:q(v)\geq 0,\sum_{v}q(v)=1\right\}</annotation></semantics></math>. It is easy to see that maximising the objective in Equation (<a href="#S2.E2" title="In Deriving Solution Conditions for Equation (). ‣ 2.2 Decoding as Distributional Optimisation ‣ 2 Decoding, Sampling and Optimisation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) can be equivalently rewritten as a minimisation problem, such that:</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}^{\star}=\arg\min_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}(\lambda\Omega(q)-\langle q,s_{t}\rangle)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}^{\star}=\arg\min_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}(\lambda\Omega(q)-\langle q,s_{t}\rangle).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Assuming that <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega(q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega(q)</annotation></semantics></math> is convex<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
                
                
                
              The convexity of <math id="footnote2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega(q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega(q)</annotation></semantics></math> is typical. As we show later, many special cases of LLM decoding strategies stem from different convex choices of <math id="footnote2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega(q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega(q)</annotation></semantics></math>.</span></span></span>, the minimisation problem we just derived (Equation (<a href="#S2.E3" title="In Deriving Solution Conditions for Equation (). ‣ 2.2 Decoding as Distributional Optimisation ‣ 2 Decoding, Sampling and Optimisation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>)) is simply a “convex - linear” minimisation objective for which clean optimality conditions are easily attainable. What makes solving the problem in Equation (<a href="#S2.E3" title="In Deriving Solution Conditions for Equation (). ‣ 2.2 Decoding as Distributional Optimisation ‣ 2 Decoding, Sampling and Optimisation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>) hard is the existence of the constraint set <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta(\mathcal{V})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta(\mathcal{V})</annotation></semantics></math>. If we were to ignore those constraints, we could just set the derivative to zero, like in unconstrained calculus, and proceed. However, the existence of those constraints means we must be more careful: we are minimising over a restricted set, so we should take those into account.</p>
<table id="S2.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><span id="S2.Ex8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath" style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;">But what do those constraints <span id="S2.Ex8.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_underline"><em id="S2.Ex8.1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">actually mean</em>?</span></span></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.4" class="ltx_p">Our constraints in <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Delta({\mathcal{V}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Delta({\mathcal{V}})</annotation></semantics></math> are not fancy at all. They are pretty simple! All they do is make <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> a valid probability distribution. In detail, when we say <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q\in\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q\in\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math>, we really mean the following two properties should hold:</p>
<ul id="S2.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S2.I3.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{v}q(v)=1\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>v</mi></msub><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{v}q(v)=1\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> Forcing <math id="S2.I3.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> to be a probability distribution that sums to 1 across all realisations of the random variable; and</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S2.I3.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(v)\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(v)\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="S2.I3.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v\in\mathcal{V}\rightarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">→</mo><mphantom></mphantom></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v\in\mathcal{V}\rightarrow</annotation></semantics></math> You can’t have negative <math id="S2.I3.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> values on any <math id="S2.I3.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v\in\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v\in\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.5" class="ltx_p">As is tradition in mathematical derivations, we begin by pretending the inconvenient part does not exist, ignore the second condition (<math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(v)\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(v)\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math>), and come back to it later. So pretend for a moment that <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(v)</annotation></semantics></math> can be any real numbers as long as they sum to 1. Here, our optimisation problem becomes:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\min_{q}\mathcal{J}(q)\equiv\lambda\Omega(q)-\sum_{v}q(v)s_{t}(v),\quad\text{s.t.}\sum_{v}q(v)=1." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mi>q</mi></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒥</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>≡</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em">−</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>v</mi></munder><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mtext>s.t.</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>v</mi></munder><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\min_{q}\mathcal{J}(q)\equiv\lambda\Omega(q)-\sum_{v}q(v)s_{t}(v),\quad\text{s.t.}\sum_{v}q(v)=1.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.6" class="ltx_p">Now, we really, really want to take derivatives and set them to zero. Sadly, there is a constraint! A standard trick is: <em id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.6.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">add the constraint into the objective with a “price” <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math></em>. This gives us what every constrained optimisation problem eventually produces, the Lagrangian:</p>
<table id="S2.Ex10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(q,\eta)={\lambda\Omega(q)}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}(1)}}-\sum_{v}q(v)s_{t}(v)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}(2)}}+\underbrace{\eta\left(\sum_{v}q(v)-1\right)}_{\text{The Constraint Penalty}}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}(3)}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>η</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">1</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em">−</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>v</mi></munder><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">2</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><munderover><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mrow><mrow><munder><mo lspace="0em" movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mi>v</mi></munder><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="true">⏟</mo></munder><mtext>The Constraint Penalty</mtext><mrow><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">(</mo><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF">3</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#0000FF;" mathcolor="#0000FF" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></munderover></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(q,\eta)={\lambda\Omega(q)}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}(1)}}-\sum_{v}q(v)s_{t}(v)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}(2)}}+\underbrace{\eta\left(\sum_{v}q(v)-1\right)}_{\text{The Constraint Penalty}}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}(3)}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.7" class="ltx_p">We now have an unconstrained objective, which allows us to deploy one of the great discoveries of the last century: the gradient. Let us do that! Let us take the partial derivatives of <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}(q,\eta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>η</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}(q,\eta)</annotation></semantics></math> with respect to <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(v)</annotation></semantics></math>. Doing so, term-by-term, we get:</p>

</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">So on the stationary point <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>, we get this condition:</p>
<table id="S2.EGx7" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\lambda\frac{\partial}{\partial q(v)}\Omega_{q(v)}(q^{\star}_{t})(v)-s_{t}(v)+\eta=0\quad\implies\quad s_{t}(v)-\lambda\frac{\partial}{\partial q(v)}\Omega(q_{t}^{\star})(v)=\eta,\ \ \ \forall v\in\mathcal{V}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>η</mi></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mo stretchy="false">⟹</mo><mspace style="width:1em;" width="1em"></mspace><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>η</mi></mrow><mo rspace="1.667em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mo rspace="0.167em">∀</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\lambda\frac{\partial}{\partial q(v)}\Omega_{q(v)}(q^{\star}_{t})(v)-s_{t}(v)+\eta=0\quad\implies\quad s_{t}(v)-\lambda\frac{\partial}{\partial q(v)}\Omega(q_{t}^{\star})(v)=\eta,\ \ \ \forall v\in\mathcal{V}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">It is easy“ish” to interpret the condition in Equation (<a href="#S2.E4" title="In Deriving Solution Conditions for Equation (). ‣ 2.2 Decoding as Distributional Optimisation ‣ 2 Decoding, Sampling and Optimisation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>). It simply says that for every token <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math>, the quantity <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}(v)-\lambda\frac{\partial}{\partial q(v)}\Omega(q_{t}^{\star})(v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}(v)-\lambda\frac{\partial}{\partial q(v)}\Omega(q_{t}^{\star})(v)</annotation></semantics></math> must be the same constant <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\eta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>η</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\eta</annotation></semantics></math>. This is a “balancing” condition created by the fact that probabilities must sum to 1.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Getting the Inequality Back.</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">At this stage, we have derived a general condition, but we should not forget about our previous promise! We still have to enforce <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(v)\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(v)\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> because some solutions to Equation (<a href="#S2.E4" title="In Deriving Solution Conditions for Equation (). ‣ 2.2 Decoding as Distributional Optimisation ‣ 2 Decoding, Sampling and Optimisation" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>) can give negative <math id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}^{\star}(v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}^{\star}(v)</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S2.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="573.28" overflow="visible" version="1.1"
