<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.6" class="ltx_p">To write in a vectorised form that is amenable to implementation, we define the following as the vector of partial derivatives:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx20" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.E12"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E12.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\bm{g}_{j}=\left[\frac{\partial f(q_{j})}{\partial q^{(1)}},\dots,\frac{\partial f(q_{j})}{\partial q^{(n)}}\right]^{\mathsf{T}}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝒈</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mstyle></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow><mi>𝖳</mi></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\bm{g}_{j}=\left[\frac{\partial f(q_{j})}{\partial q^{(1)}},\dots,\frac{\partial f(q_{j})}{\partial q^{(n)}}\right]^{\mathsf{T}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(12)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.7" class="ltx_p">The numerator of Equation (<a href="#S4.E11" title="In Entropic Distance-Generating Functions over the Simplex. ‣ 4.2 Bregman Divergences &amp; Mirror Ascent ‣ 4 Going Beyond Current Decoders" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a>) is thus:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex77" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex77.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Numerator}=q_{j}\odot\exp(\eta\bm{g}_{j})," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>Numerator</mtext><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝒈</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Numerator}=q_{j}\odot\exp(\eta\bm{g}_{j}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.8" class="ltx_p">with <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\odot" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>⊙</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\odot</annotation></semantics></math> being the Hadamard or element-wise product. The denominator is simply the <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{L}_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>L</mtext><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{L}_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> norm of the numerator: <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{Denominator}=||q_{j}\odot\exp(\eta\bm{g}_{j})||_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mtext>Denominator</mtext><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝒈</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{Denominator}=||q_{j}\odot\exp(\eta\bm{g}_{j})||_{1}</annotation></semantics></math>. Therefore:</p>
<table id="S4.E13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{\scriptsize\color[rgb]{0.0508,0.2773,0.6328}``Mirror Ascent Update'' \hskip 7.00002pt}q_{j+1}=\frac{\text{Numerator}}{\text{Denominator}}=\frac{q_{j}\odot\exp(\eta\bm{g}_{j})}{||q_{j}\odot\exp(\eta\bm{g}_{j})||_{1}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mtext style="--ltx-fg-color:#0D47A1;" class="ltx_font_smallcaps" mathcolor="#0D47A1" mathsize="0.700em">“Mirror Ascent Update” </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mtext>Numerator</mtext><mtext>Denominator</mtext></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝒈</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝒈</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{\scriptsize\color[rgb]{0.0508,0.2773,0.6328}``Mirror Ascent Update'' \hskip 7.00002pt}q_{j+1}=\frac{\text{Numerator}}{\text{Denominator}}=\frac{q_{j}\odot\exp(\eta\bm{g}_{j})}{||q_{j}\odot\exp(\eta\bm{g}_{j})||_{1}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(13)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, computing <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\exp(\eta\frac{\partial f}{\partial q^{(i)}})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\exp(\eta\frac{\partial f}{\partial q^{(i)}})</annotation></semantics></math> directly can lead to numerical overflow if the gradients are large. To prevent this, we use the Log-Sum-Exp trick by subtracting the maximum value <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=\max(\eta\bm{g}_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝒈</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=\max(\eta\bm{g}_{j})</annotation></semantics></math> from the exponents. Because the sum normalises the update, this shift cancels out mathematically but ensures the computer always handles values <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\leq 1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\leq 1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection" style="font-size:120%;--ltx-fg-color:#808080;">4.3  Use Case: Best-of-K Samplers</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We have done a lot of groundwork: we reframed decoding as optimisation on the simplex, re-derived several classical decoders as closed-form special cases, and introduced mirror ascent as a practical solver when closed forms are unavailable. The point of all this was not just unification for its own sake. It was to argue that an optimisation view gives us a principled design language for decoding: samplers are best understood as regularisers (and constraints), and new decoding behaviour should be obtained by writing down the objective we actually want to optimise. To make good on this claim, we now present a concrete use case. We introduce a new regulariser, Best-of-K (BoK), designed for settings where we draw multiple samples and care about coverage of high-quality alternatives, not just the properties of a single draw. BoK drops into our master problem as a plug-in term, and mirror ascent gives an immediate, implementable algorithm.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The motivation is simple: many modern pipelines do not sample once; they sample
K times (self-consistency, rejection sampling, reranking, verifier-based selection, etc.). In that regime, the decoder is no longer judged by the quality of a single draw, but by what the set of K draws contains. Standard decoders were not designed for this: they often waste budget by repeatedly sampling the same high-probability continuation, while allocating too little mass to plausible alternatives that are individually unlikely but collectively valuable when we have multiple tries. What we want instead is a decoding distribution <math id="S4.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}^{\star}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}^{\star}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> that makes good options show up at least once within K samples, i.e., that explicitly trades off model score against multi-sample coverage. This is exactly the behaviour our framework is built to express: we define a coverage utility for K draws, convert it into a regulariser, and plug it into the master objective to obtain the Best-of-K (BoK) sampler.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The hit probability.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Fix a token <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v\in\mathcal{V}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v\in\mathcal{V}</annotation></semantics></math> and suppose we draw <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> i.i.d. samples from a decoding distribution <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math>. The probability that we <em id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">never</em> sample <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> is <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(1-q(v))^{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>K</mi></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(1-q(v))^{K}</annotation></semantics></math>. Therefore, the probability that <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> appears <em id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">at least once</em> among the <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> samples is:</p>
<table id="S4.E14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{P}\textrm{r}[\text{$v$ appears at least once in $K$ samples}]=1-(1-q(v))^{K}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>𝐏</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>r</mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mtext> appears at least once in </mtext><mi>K</mi><mtext> samples</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>K</mi></msup></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{P}\textrm{r}[\text{$v$ appears at least once in $K$ samples}]=1-(1-q(v))^{K}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(14)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This quantity captures what single-sample decoding objectives ignore: in a multi-sample regime, even moderately small probabilities can become valuable if they increase the chance of seeing a useful alternative at least once.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Summing Equation (<a href="#S4.E14" title="In The hit probability. ‣ 4.3 Use Case: Best-of-K Samplers ‣ 4 Going Beyond Current Decoders" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>) over all tokens yields a notion of total coverage. However, we do not want to reward covering junk tokens equally with high-quality ones, so we introduce nonnegative importance weights <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}(v)\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}(v)\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> and define the <em id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">weighted <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>-coverage</em>:</p>
<table id="S4.E15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U}_{K,t}(q):=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}w_{t}(v)\Big(1-(1-q(v))^{K}\Big)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">:=</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>K</mi></msup></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{U}_{K,t}(q):=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}w_{t}(v)\Big(1-(1-q(v))^{K}\Big).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(15)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Intuitively, <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U}_{K,t}(q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{U}_{K,t}(q)</annotation></semantics></math> is large when: <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">i)</span> We allocate mass to many tokens that we care about (large <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}(v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}(v)</annotation></semantics></math>), and <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ii)</span> this mass is sufficient for them to be hit at least once within <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> samples. In practice, <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w_{t}(v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w_{t}(v)</annotation></semantics></math> can be any nonnegative proxy for “how much we would like to see token <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>v</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v</annotation></semantics></math> among <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> draws” (e.g., a monotone function of the model score <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{t}(v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{t}(v)</annotation></semantics></math>, a Top-M indicator, or a softened rank-based weight).</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">A useful property of the hit probability <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1-(1-q(v))^{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>K</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1-(1-q(v))^{K}</annotation></semantics></math> is that it exhibits <em id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">diminishing returns</em>:
its marginal gain decreases as <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(v)</annotation></semantics></math> grows. Indeed:</p>
<table id="S4.Ex78" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.Ex78.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\frac{\partial}{\partial q(v)}\Big(1-(1-q(v))^{K}\Big)=K(1-q(v))^{K-1}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mfrac><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>K</mi></msup></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\partial}{\partial q(v)}\Big(1-(1-q(v))^{K}\Big)=K(1-q(v))^{K-1},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">which is strictly decreasing in <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q(v)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q(v)</annotation></semantics></math> for <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K&gt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K&gt;1</annotation></semantics></math>.
Thus, BoK has an inherent “anti-collapse” bias: it is more rewarding to allocate probability mass
to under-covered but valuable tokens than to keep increasing the mass of tokens that are already
likely to appear. This is exactly the multi-sample behaviour we want.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">BoK as a regulariser.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Maximising <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U}_{K,t}(q)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{U}_{K,t}(q)</annotation></semantics></math> alone would encourage spreading probability mass too widely, including onto implausible tokens.
To keep the decoder anchored to the model, we combine coverage with a KL trust region around the model distribution
<math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> and define the BoK regulariser</p>
<table id="S4.E16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E16.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\Omega^{(\mathrm{BoK})}_{t}(q):=\mathrm{KL}(q\|p_{t})-\beta\,\mathcal{U}_{K,t}(q)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>BoK</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>:=</mo><mi>KL</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>β</mi><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega^{(\mathrm{BoK})}_{t}(q):=\mathrm{KL}(q\|p_{t})-\beta\,\mathcal{U}_{K,t}(q),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(16)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta\geq 0" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta\geq 0</annotation></semantics></math> controls how strongly we reward coverage.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Plugging Equation (<a href="#S4.E16" title="In BoK as a regulariser. ‣ 4.3 Use Case: Best-of-K Samplers ‣ 4 Going Beyond Current Decoders" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>) into our master problem yields the BoK decoding objective:</p>
<table id="S4.EGx21" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S4.Ex79"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex79.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle q_{t}^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle q_{t}^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.Ex79.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\arg\max_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\Big[\langle q,s_{t}\rangle-\lambda\,\Omega^{(\mathrm{BoK})}_{t}(q)\Big]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></munder><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">[</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>BoK</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\arg\max_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\Big[\langle q,s_{t}\rangle-\lambda\,\Omega^{(\mathrm{BoK})}_{t}(q)\Big]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S4.E17"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_eqn_cell"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S4.E17.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\displaystyle=\arg\max_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\Big[\langle q,s_{t}\rangle-\lambda\,\mathrm{KL}(q\|p_{t})+\bar{\beta}\,\mathcal{U}_{K,t}(q)\Big]," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>arg</mi><munder><mi>max</mi><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></munder><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">[</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>λ</mi><mi>KL</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">]</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\arg\max_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\Big[\langle q,s_{t}\rangle-\lambda\,\mathrm{KL}(q\|p_{t})+\bar{\beta}\,\mathcal{U}_{K,t}(q)\Big],</annotation></semantics></math></td>

<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">with <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bar{\beta}:=\lambda\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>β</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bar{\beta}:=\lambda\beta</annotation></semantics></math> for convenience.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Mirror-Ascent Update for <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega^{(\mathrm{BoK})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>BoK</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega^{(\mathrm{BoK})}</annotation></semantics></math>.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Unfortunately, exact closed-forms are hard to come by for <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\Omega^{(\mathrm{BoK})}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">Ω</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>BoK</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\Omega^{(\mathrm{BoK})}</annotation></semantics></math>. Thus, we make use of our mirror ascent update rule in Equation <a href="#S4.E13" title="In Entropic Distance-Generating Functions over the Simplex. ‣ 4.2 Bregman Divergences &amp; Mirror Ascent ‣ 4 Going Beyond Current Decoders" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>. For a single decoding step, BoK-regularised objective is defined as:</p>
<table id="S4.E18" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E18.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="f(q)=\langle q,s_{t}\rangle-\lambda\,\mathrm{KL}(q\|p_{t})+\bar{\beta}\,\mathcal{U}_{K,t}(q)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">⟨</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">⟩</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mi>λ</mi><mi>KL</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∥</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>β</mi><mo>¯</mo></mover><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(q)=\langle q,s_{t}\rangle-\lambda\,\mathrm{KL}(q\|p_{t})+\bar{\beta}\,\mathcal{U}_{K,t}(q),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(18)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t}\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">Δ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t}\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})</annotation></semantics></math> is the reference/model distribution, and</p>
<table id="S4.E19" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E19.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{U}_{K,t}(q)=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}w_{t}(v^{(i)})\Big(1-(1-q^{(i)})^{K}\Big)." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒰</mi><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><munder><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo><mrow><mi>v</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi></mrow></munder><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>v</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>K</mi></msup></mrow><mo maxsize="1.600em" minsize="1.600em">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{U}_{K,t}(q)=\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}w_{t}(v^{(i)})\Big(1-(1-q^{(i)})^{K}\Big).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(19)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.3" class="ltx_p">Define the vector of partial derivatives at iterate <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> as</p>
<table id="S4.E20" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E20.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{g}_{j}=\left[\frac{\partial f(q_{j})}{\partial q^{(1)}},\dots,\frac{\partial f(q_{j})}{\partial q^{(|\mathcal{V}|)}}\right]^{\mathsf{T}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>𝒈</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo>[</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><msup><mi>q</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒱</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow><mi>𝖳</mi></msup></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{g}_{j}=\left[\frac{\partial f(q_{j})}{\partial q^{(1)}},\dots,\frac{\partial f(q_{j})}{\partial q^{(|\mathcal{V}|)}}\right]^{\mathsf{T}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(20)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.4" class="ltx_p">For each coordinate <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i\in\{1,\dots,n\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i\in\{1,\dots,n\}</annotation></semantics></math>, the partial derivative admits the closed form (we denote <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w^{(i)}_{t}=w_{t}(v^{(i)})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>v</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w^{(i)}_{t}=w_{t}(v^{(i)})</annotation></semantics></math>)</p>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Of course, with <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{g}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒈</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{g}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> as in Equation (<a href="#S4.E20" title="In Mirror-Ascent Update for Ω^(BoK). ‣ 4.3 Use Case: Best-of-K Samplers ‣ 4 Going Beyond Current Decoders" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">20</span></a>), the update can be written compactly as:</p>
<table id="S4.E23" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S4.E23.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{j+1}=\frac{q_{j}\odot\exp(\eta\bm{g}_{j})}{\|q_{j}\odot\exp(\eta\bm{g}_{j})\|_{1}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝒈</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⊙</mo><mrow><mi>exp</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝒈</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">‖</mo></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{j+1}=\frac{q_{j}\odot\exp(\eta\bm{g}_{j})}{\|q_{j}\odot\exp(\eta\bm{g}_{j})\|_{1}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(23)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ Mirror-Ascent Update for Ω^(BoK). ‣ 4.3 Use Case: Best-of-K Samplers ‣ 4 Going Beyond Current Decoders" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> summarises how to compute the BoK decoding distribution at a single time step.
We initialise the iterate with the model distribution <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{0}=p_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{0}=p_{t}</annotation></semantics></math> (a natural warm-start), then perform <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="J" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>J</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">J</annotation></semantics></math> mirror-ascent steps.
Each step computes the vector of partial derivatives <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\bm{g}_{j}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>𝒈</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\bm{g}_{j}</annotation></semantics></math> using the closed form in Equation (<a href="#S4.E21" title="In Mirror-Ascent Update for Ω^(BoK). ‣ 4.3 Use Case: Best-of-K Samplers ‣ 4 Going Beyond Current Decoders" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a>), and applies the
multiplicative update in Equation (<a href="#S4.E23" title="In Mirror-Ascent Update for Ω^(BoK). ‣ 4.3 Use Case: Best-of-K Samplers ‣ 4 Going Beyond Current Decoders" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">23</span></a>), and renormalises to stay on the simplex.
In practice, we implement the update with a Log-Sum-Exp stabilisation by subtracting <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=\max(\eta\bm{g}_{j})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>η</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>𝒈</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=\max(\eta\bm{g}_{j})</annotation></semantics></math> before exponentiating.</p>
</div>

                <span id="alg1.l5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> <math id="alg1.l5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i=1,2,\dots,n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i=1,2,\dots,n</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l5.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>

<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_subsection" style="font-size:120%;--ltx-fg-color:#808080;">4.4  Use Case Evaluation: How good are BoK Samplers?</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate the BoK Sampler as a practical, decoding-time regulariser for improving multi-sample generation without additional training or external verifiers. The evaluation is designed to answer three questions: (i) whether BoK improves solution quality over standard sampling baselines; (ii) whether the gains are robust across decoding temperatures and different hyperparameter choices in the underlying optimisation; and (iii) what compute overhead is incurred when solving the BoK objective with mirror ascent. Our main finding is that BoK consistently improves or matches standard decoding across tasks and models, with the largest gains appearing in higher-temperature regimes where vanilla sampling is more diverse but less reliable. BoK leverages the regularised objective to retain diversity while increasing the chance of sampling high-quality alternatives with only a small computational overhead.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Accuracy across temperatures for Qwen2.5-Math-7B on MATH500, GPQA, and HumanEval. We report Base, Top-K (K=50), and BoK with three representative <math id="S4.T1.m16" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\beta,\lambda)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>λ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\beta,\lambda)</annotation></semantics></math> settings, illustrating robustness across both temperature and hyperparameters.</figcaption>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Accuracy across temperatures for Qwen2.5-7B on MATH500, GPQA, and HumanEval (same baselines and BoK settings as Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.4 Use Case Evaluation: How good are BoK Samplers? ‣ 4 Going Beyond Current Decoders" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).</figcaption>

<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Experimental setup.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate BoK on a math-specialised model <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Qwen2.5-Math-7B</span> and a general-purpose model <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Qwen2.5-7B</span>, across three complementary benchmarks spanning math, QA, and code: <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MATH500</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>]</cite>, <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GPQA-diamond</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>]</cite>, and <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">HumanEval</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>. We compare BoK against standard autoregressive sampling (Base) from the model distribution at temperature <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, and Top-K, sampling restricted to the top-<math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> tokens per step with renormalisation (we fix <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K{=}50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K{=}50</annotation></semantics></math> across tasks and temperatures). All methods use the same prompts (Qwen default prompts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>) and evaluation scripts, the same maximum generation length <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\max}{=}3072" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3072</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\max}{=}3072</annotation></semantics></math> with early stopping on <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">EOS</span>, and the same random-seed protocol.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results and Analysis.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We implement the BoK sampler following Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ Mirror-Ascent Update for Ω^(BoK). ‣ 4.3 Use Case: Best-of-K Samplers ‣ 4 Going Beyond Current Decoders" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, using mirror-ascent updates to compute a per-step sampling distribution <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}^{\star}(\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}^{\star}(\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> that increases exploration via the coverage utility while remaining anchored to the base model through KL regularisation (Eq. (<a href="#S4.E17" title="In BoK as a regulariser. ‣ 4.3 Use Case: Best-of-K Samplers ‣ 4 Going Beyond Current Decoders" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>)). In particular, <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> controls the strength of the coverage reward, and <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> controls the strength of KL anchoring toward the reference distribution <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>. Across tasks and models, BoK matches or improves upon Base and Top-K sampling in most settings, as shown in Tables <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.4 Use Case Evaluation: How good are BoK Samplers? ‣ 4 Going Beyond Current Decoders" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.4 Use Case Evaluation: How good are BoK Samplers? ‣ 4 Going Beyond Current Decoders" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The gains are most pronounced at higher temperatures, where vanilla sampling becomes more diverse but less reliable. For <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Qwen2.5-Math-7B</span> on <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">MATH500</span> at <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau{=}0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau{=}0.9</annotation></semantics></math>, BoK increases accuracy from 53.0% to 71.6% (+18.6%) and exceeds Top-K at 56.2% by +15.4%. We observe a similar pattern on <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">GPQA</span> and <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">HumanEval</span>, where BoK improves over the baselines at <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau{=}0.9" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau{=}0.9</annotation></semantics></math> by +6.06% and +14.64%. Similar improvements hold for <span id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Qwen2.5-7B</span>, where BoK substantially mitigates the accuracy drop at high temperatures. At lower temperatures, improvements are naturally smaller; in a few near-deterministic regimes, Base or Top-K sampling can remain slightly stronger or comparable to BoK, which is consistent with the reduced need for exploration when the model distribution is already sharply peaked.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The results also indicate that BoK is not overly sensitive to hyperparameter choice: multiple <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\beta,\lambda)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>β</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>λ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\beta,\lambda)</annotation></semantics></math> settings yield competitive performance across temperatures, with the best pair varying by task and regime. Overall, the consistent improvements across all three tested configurations suggest a stable operating region. BoK thus provides a practical and robust way to trade off diversity and reliability at decoding time without exhaustive hyperparameter search, with particularly strong benefits in high-entropy sampling settings.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">
<div id="S4.T3.3" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:276.0pt;height:28.7pt;vertical-align:-12.6pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-40.6pt,4.2pt) scale(0.772634009760952,0.772634009760952) ;">
<table id="S4.T3.3.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S4.T3.3.1.1" class="ltx_tr">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:90%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>Effect of the number of mirror-gradient steps per token on MATH500 accuracy for Qwen2.5-MATH-7B (BoK) using <math id="S4.T3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau=0.7" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>τ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.7</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau=0.7</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.T3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.01" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.01</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.T3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda=0.1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda=0.1</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Efficiency and practical deployment.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, BoK introduces only a small runtime overhead because computing the BoK-optimal distribution <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math> requires only a few mirror-ascent updates per token. All BoK results in Tables <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.4 Use Case Evaluation: How good are BoK Samplers? ‣ 4 Going Beyond Current Decoders" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> and <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.4 Use Case Evaluation: How good are BoK Samplers? ‣ 4 Going Beyond Current Decoders" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> use <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5</annotation></semantics></math> mirror-ascent steps per token. Across the three benchmarks, the additional cost remains modest relative to base decoding: on MATH500, BoK runs in 16.88s vs. 15.84s; on GPQA, 17.60s vs. 15.43s; and on HumanEval, BoK is slightly faster in our implementation (8.65s vs. 9.74s), which we attribute to shorter generations under BoK. This suggests that the mirror-ascent solver converges quickly, so only a small number of optimisation steps are required to obtain an effective <math id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q_{t}^{\star}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>t</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q_{t}^{\star}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To make this explicit, we further study the effect of the number of mirror-gradient steps per token on the MATH500 task, as shown in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Results and Analysis. ‣ 4.4 Use Case Evaluation: How good are BoK Samplers? ‣ 4 Going Beyond Current Decoders" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. There is an improvement compared with the base decoding, even with a small number of steps: using only 2 steps improves accuracy from 64.4% to 69.6% with a negligible runtime increase (15.87s), and 5 steps reach 73.0% with a still modest overhead (16.88s). Increasing the number of steps beyond 5 yields only marginal changes in accuracy while steadily increasing runtime. Overall, these results indicate that BoK remains effective with a small, fixed number of mirror-ascent steps, making it suitable for practical decoding-time use.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_font_bold ltx_title_section" style="font-size:144%;">5  Conclusion and Future Work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We argued that decoding should not be viewed as a collection of disconnected heuristics.
Instead, many widely used decoding rules arise as exact solutions to a single optimisation template on the probability simplex,
where different decoding behaviours correspond to different regularisers and feasible sets.
This perspective unifies classical procedures (e.g., greedy, Softmax, Top-K/Top-P, and sparse decoders) under one “Master” problem,
and makes explicit the role of optimality conditions in determining which tokens become active or inactive.
When closed-form solutions are unavailable, we showed that mirror ascent provides a principled, simplex-native solver whose updates preserve
valid distributions by construction.
Finally, to demonstrate that the framework is not merely explanatory, we introduced a concrete use case, the Best-of-K (BoK) regulariser, which
directly targets multi-sample coverage and can be implemented with the same mirror-ascent machinery.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The optimisation view suggests several promising directions.
First, while we focused on per-step decoding, it would be natural to extend the framework to <em id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">sequence-level</em> objectives that couple decisions across time <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>,
e.g., enforcing coverage, length, or style constraints globally rather than locally.
Second, BoK illustrates how multi-sample utilities can be encoded as regularisers; a broader family of <em id="S5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">compute-aware</em> objectives could be explored,
including utilities that model downstream reranking, verifier selection, or self-consistency more explicitly <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>, <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>, <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite>.
Third, mirror ascent opens the door to richer constraint sets beyond the simplex, such as structured sparsity, group constraints, or dynamic support sets that depend on
external tools or retrieval modules <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>, <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">33</a>]</cite>.
We hope this work helps shift decoder design from folklore to first-principles objective design.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="S5.p3.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="61.26" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 670 61.26" width="670"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,61.26) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#404040;" fill="#404040" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 7.87 L 0 53.38 C 0 57.73 3.53 61.26 7.87 61.26 L 662.13 61.26 C 666.48 61.26 670 57.73 670 53.38 L 670 7.87 C 670 3.53 666.48 0 662.13 0 L 7.87 0 C 3.53 0 0 3.53 0 7.87 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#FCFCFC;" fill="#FCFCFC" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 7.87 L 0 53.38 C 0 57.73 3.53 61.26 7.87 61.26 L 662.13 61.26 C 666.48 61.26 670 57.73 670 53.38 L 670 7.87 C 670 3.53 666.48 0 662.13 0 L 7.87 0 C 3.53 0 0 3.53 0 7.87 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#D9D9D9;--ltx-fill-color:#D9D9D9;--ltx-fg-color:#D9D9D9;" color="#D9D9D9" fill="#D9D9D9" stroke="#D9D9D9" stroke-width="2.0pt"><path style="fill:none" d="M 1.38 61.26 L 1.38 0"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 15.75 43.77)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:46.15em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:2.59em;font-size:10pt;" height="45.51" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="638.59"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="S5.p3.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:46.15em;">
<span id="S5.p3.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S5.p3.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="position:relative; bottom:0.2pt;--ltx-fg-color:#1A1A1A;"><img src="" id="S5.p3.pic1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_missing ltx_missing_image" alt="[Uncaptioned image]"></span><span id="S5.p3.pic1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#1A1A1A;">

              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
